name: PSP / payment-orchestration real-time risk
category: Adjacent — processor / orchestration-side risk (distinct from card-issuer or lender)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Processor- / orchestrator-side real-time risk and routing decisioning (PSPs, payment orchestrators, large-merchant in-house payment switches)
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A PSP, payment orchestrator, or large merchant's in-house payment switch must decide in roughly 20–50 ms — inside the broader 100–200 ms authorization budget — which acquirer/PSP/network rail to route an inbound charge to, whether to retry on failure, and whether to step the transaction up (e.g., 3DS) using fresh per-merchant / per-BIN / per-gateway / per-route success-rate and risk features.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: Three concrete jobs an engineer on the routing / risk side of a PSP or orchestrator is trying to accomplish: (1) Pick the best route at auth time — score N candidate (acquirer, MID, rail) combinations against fresh per-(BIN, acquirer) success-rate, per-acquirer latency p95, per-acquirer current health, and per-(merchant, decline_code) retry-eligibility features, and return the chosen route within a 20–50 ms routing-decision sub-budget (the rest of the ~100 ms auth budget goes to vault, connector translation, and the upstream/downstream PSP itself). The control-theoretic / multi-armed-bandit literature (e.g., the JUSPAY 2025 arXiv paper, Razorpay's 2021 Smart Routing paper) treats this exactly as a stateful real-time-feature problem. (2) Detect and short-circuit card-testing / BIN-attack bursts at the orchestrator before they fan out to multiple acquirers — sliding-window counters per (BIN, merchant), per IP, per device, and per (card_hash, merchant) detect 'dozens of small auths in seconds' and trigger throttling, decline, or step-up before the issuer sees the second wave. (3) Detect cascading retry / failover storms and gateway-health degradation in real time — per-(acquirer, decline_code) velocities, per-acquirer rolling success-rate, and per-acquirer latency distributions feed a circuit-breaker that opens within seconds of a success-rate dip (industry best-in-class: switchover under 200 ms; AI-driven detection within seconds of the dip beginning) so traffic moves off a sick provider before customers feel it.
domain_fit.event_shapes: Typical events that would land in beava as @bv.event records on the orchestrator side: route_request {ts, request_id, merchant_id, card_hash, bin, last4, amount_cents, currency, channel, mcc, ship_country, ip, device_id, is_3ds, customer_id}, route_decision {ts, request_id, chosen_acquirer, chosen_mid, candidate_set, decision_reason, decision_ms}, gateway_response {ts, request_id, acquirer, mid, auth_decision, decline_code, processor_rt_ms, network_used}, retry_attempt {ts, request_id, attempt_n, prior_acquirer, new_acquirer, prior_decline_code}, three_ds_outcome {ts, request_id, acs_decision, frictionless, acs_rt_ms}, settlement_outcome {ts, request_id, settled, captured, refunded}, chargeback {ts, request_id, reason_code, liable_party}, fraud_label {ts, request_id, is_fraud, source, t_minus_days}. Crucially, beava on the orchestrator only ever sees tokens (card_hash, BIN, last4) so it stays out of the PCI-DSS cardholder-data environment (CDE) by construction — the PAN lives in the orchestrator's vault, not beava.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Aggregations expressed in beava @bv.table primitives, by entity grain: (acquirer, BIN) → rolling approval-rate (1m / 5m / 1h / 24h sliding), p95 latency distribution, count(declines, 5m), count by decline_code (5m / 1h); acquirer → rolling success-rate, latency distribution (HDR / t-digest if available), count(timeouts, 1m), share-of-traffic; merchant_id → rolling decline-rate (1m / 1h / 24h), velocity of charge_attempt (1m / 5m / 1h), chargeback-rate (rolling 7d / 30d / 90d for PSD2 TRA accounting), count(card_testing_indicator, 5m); (merchant_id, BIN) → BIN-attack indicator: count distinct card_hash in 1m / 5m on the same BIN at the same merchant; card_hash → count(charge_attempt, 1m / 10m / 1h), count(declines, 1h), n_unique(merchant_id, 24h), n_unique(acquirer, 24h); ip / device_id → count(charge_attempt, 1m / 10m), n_unique(card_hash, 10m), n_unique(BIN, 10m) — classic explosive grains where HLL/CMS is the right shape; (acquirer, decline_code) → rolling count and rate, plus time-since-last-occurrence — feeds the retry/cascade policy ('don't retry insufficient_funds elsewhere; do retry processor_timeout'); route → rolling cost ($) per successful auth, used for cost-aware routing alongside success-rate.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Mixed and parallel. Primary keys in production orchestrator/PSP routing rigs: acquirer / connector_id, (acquirer, BIN), (acquirer, decline_code), merchant_id, (merchant_id, BIN), (merchant_id, decline_code), card_hash, bin, ip, device_id, route_id (= acquirer + MID + network rail). A single routing decision typically reads features from 6–10 of these grains in one batched call.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding dominates (1m, 5m, 10m, 1h, 24h) for live success-rate, decline-rate, latency, and velocity. Tumbling shows up for regulator-facing fraud-rate accounting (PSD2 quarterly fraud-rate reporting on a 90-day tumbling window, with tiered thresholds — e.g., 0.01% fraud-rate ceiling for the €250–500 transaction band, up to 0.13% at lower values). Session windows show up rarely on the orchestrator side (per-customer-session retry chains). Approximate aggregates (HLL for n_unique IPs/devices/cards on a BIN, CMS for top-K offending BINs/IPs, t-digest for latency p95/p99 per acquirer) are acceptable and often preferred for high-cardinality grains; exact counts are required for the PSD2-TRA fraud-rate accounting path.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Mixed. The routing-decision hot path tolerates at-least-once with idempotent counters keyed by request_id (a duplicated count of one request does not change route choice materially). The PSD2 TRA fraud-rate accounting path needs strict no-double-count or compensating reconciliation against the system of record because the 90-day quarterly fraud-rate is regulator-graded. Chargeback-liability accounting is also strict.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Routing-decision sub-budget is 20–50 ms (the route-selection step itself); the broader auth budget is ~100 ms end-to-end. Industry sources are explicit: 'the entire decision, from request arrival to PSP selection, completes in 20–50 ms'; 'sub-100ms routing decisions under load' are the design target; best-in-class orchestrators target <200 ms processing time end-to-end. Hyperswitch (open-source Rust orchestrator) reports ~25 ms application latency. Beava's published sub-millisecond TCP get_many fits inside the 20–50 ms sub-budget with two orders of magnitude of margin.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to a few seconds. Gateway-health and BIN-attack signals must surface within seconds of the underlying event — best-in-class systems 'detect success rate dips within seconds' and switch traffic 'under 200 ms' once the dip is seen. Minute-level batch features are too stale: a card-testing burst can run hundreds of attempts in seconds, and a sick acquirer can burn thousands of declines in the same window. Beava's push-on-event model gives single-digit-ms staleness, which matches the requirement directly.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Orchestrator/PSP throughput spans a wide range. Public references: payment-orchestration platforms 'designed to handle over 1,000 TPS'; Nuvei has expanded global processing to '10,000 TPS'; JUSPAY processes '200M daily transactions globally' ≈ ~2.3k TPS daily average with peaks materially higher; Stripe and global card networks process much more. Each charge generates several beava events (route_request, route_decision, gateway_response, possibly retry_attempt and three_ds_outcome), so write EPS is typically 3–5× transaction TPS. Beava's published ~684k EPS sustained on a single Apple-M4 core (TCP+msgpack+parallel=16) comfortably exceeds the single-tenant requirements of mid-sized PSPs, regional orchestrators, and large-merchant in-house switches; only the very largest global PSPs / networks push past a single-binary budget. [uncertain] exact published EPS for Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com routing tiers (not publicly disclosed).
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Balanced to slightly write-heavy. Every routing decision is one batched read (6–10 entity grains × tens of features), followed by 2–4 writes as the request progresses (route_request → route_decision → gateway_response → optional retry/3DS). A reasonable rule of thumb is 1 batched-read per 2–4 writes; card-testing storms skew it strongly toward write-heavy on the (BIN, merchant), card_hash, and IP grains.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Order-of-magnitude per buyer. A mid-sized PSP / orchestrator with ~100k–1M active merchants × ~50 connector slots × ~50 features per (merchant, acquirer) grain × ~16 bytes per counter ≈ 4–40 GB hot state, with the high-cardinality (card_hash, ip, device_id) grains adding another 10–50 GB depending on HLL/CMS sketch sizing — well inside a single beava box. A global PSP at Stripe/Adyen scale (billions of cards, thousands of connectors, dozens of regions) pushes into the low TB range and would exceed today's single-binary in-memory ceiling, requiring sharding or multi-region partitioning.
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Bounded on acquirer (tens to low hundreds per buyer) and (acquirer, decline_code) (tens to low hundreds × small enum of decline codes), slowly-growing on merchant_id and BIN, explosive on card_hash, ip, and device_id. The bounded/slowly-growing grains tolerate exact counters; the explosive grains are exactly where HLL n_unique and CMS top-K sketches are the right shape (e.g., 'how many distinct card_hashes attempted on this BIN in the last 5 minutes' is naturally HLL).
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Mixed TTLs. Gateway-health and per-(acquirer, BIN) success-rate windows: seconds to hours. Per-merchant velocity and BIN-attack indicators: minutes to a day. Per-merchant chargeback / fraud-rate accounting for PSD2 TRA: 90-day rolling (quarterly tumbling) plus settlement-cycle lookbacks. Chargeback-liability counters: 540 days+ depending on scheme. Beava's WAL + snapshot model fits the seconds-to-day hot tier cleanly; the multi-quarter and multi-year tails belong in a system of record and can be reconciled from beava's stream.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 30–100 features per routing decision is typical. The Razorpay 2021 'AI-powered Smart Routing' arXiv paper and Stripe's documented Radar architecture (hundreds of features per fraud decision; ~200 features in the SEPA Shepherd model) bracket the range. The routing decision specifically tends to be smaller than the full fraud decision (40–80 features) because route selection focuses on per-acquirer / per-BIN / per-merchant health and historical success-rate, not the full per-card behavioural profile.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe is table-stakes for the routing/health path; losing the last few seconds of per-acquirer success-rate counters during a node failure creates a brief blind spot during which routing falls back to defaults (still safe, just sub-optimal). Regulator-grade durability is required for the PSD2 TRA fraud-rate accounting path and for chargeback-liability counters, which must be reconcilable to the orchestrator's system of record DB. Beava's WAL + periodic snapshot + refuse-on-network-FS matches the crash-safe tier; for regulator-grade, beava must be paired with a durable downstream sink (Kafka, Postgres CDC, S3) so the 90-day fraud-rate accounting is independently auditable.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary regional / single-binary-per-tenant fits a mid-sized PSP, a regional payment orchestrator, or a large-merchant in-house switch cleanly (Hyperswitch's published architecture is single-region per deployment and ~25 ms application latency on a single core). Multi-region active-active with strong consistency is NOT a fit today: beava has no in-process sharding and no cross-region replication in v0, so a global orchestrator with merchants on three continents and authorization paths in each cannot use a single beava box as the source of truth for gateway-health state; an external coordination layer or per-region beava with eventual reconciliation would be required.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Primary: the payments-platform engineering team (Head of Payments Engineering, VP of Payments, Payments Infrastructure Lead) at PSPs, payment orchestrators, and large merchants with in-house payment switches. Secondary: the payments-data-science / ML team that builds the routing model, and the risk team that owns BIN-attack and card-testing rules. The risk team is more central at orchestrators (Gr4vy, Primer, Spreedly) where 'real-time risk decisioning' is sold as a feature; the platform team is more central at large in-house switches (Uber, Airbnb, Booking).
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Large and growing. Adyen, Stripe, Checkout.com, Worldpay/FIS, Fiserv, Nuvei, and JUSPAY operate at hundreds of billions to trillions of USD TPV annually (JUSPAY publicly cites >$670B annual TPV; Stripe processes >$1.4T TPV). The payment-orchestration sub-segment alone is forecast in the high-single-digit-billion USD range with 20%+ CAGR (multiple analyst reports). Specialist orchestrators (Primer, Gr4vy, Spreedly, Corefy, Solidgate, IXOPAY, Cellulant) have raised significant venture capital; Primer is the most-cited 'orchestration 2.0' vendor. Adyen RevenueAccelerate and Stripe Authorization Boost / Adaptive Acceptance are public, named products built on exactly this kind of streaming-feature substrate — Adyen reports 26% cost savings and 0.22% authorization uplift in an enterprise pilot; Stripe cites 10% of false declines recovered, 'billions of dollars globally'. [uncertain] specific revenue figures for the orchestration sub-segment (estimates vary).
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: Four forces: (1) Approval-rate revenue lift — a 1–3 point lift in approval rate is worth tens to hundreds of millions of dollars for a mid-to-large PSP or merchant; ML-driven routing demonstrably delivers this (Adyen 26% cost savings, Stripe 8% fraud reduction + 1–2% auth uplift, JUSPAY ~1.15% success-rate improvement vs rule-based, third-party ML routers reporting 96.7% vs 94.1% in A/B tests). (2) Card-testing / BIN-attack pressure — losses and reputational damage from card-testing surges on the orchestrator's merchants drive 'we need real-time velocity counters now' procurement. (3) Regulation — PSD2 SCA TRA exemption depends on the orchestrator's quarterly fraud-rate staying under tiered EBA thresholds (0.01%–0.13%), which forces auditable real-time + accumulated fraud-rate accounting; PSD3 is expected to tighten thresholds further (2026–2027). (4) Resilience — gateway downtime + cascading-retry storms are existential reputational events for orchestrators; sub-second detection is now table stakes (industry best-in-class: <200 ms switchover, 'within seconds' detection).
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: PCI-DSS v4.0.1 — beava must NEVER touch PAN or sensitive authentication data (SAD); the orchestrator's vault keeps PAN out of beava's scope by passing only tokens (card_hash, BIN, last4); buyers will want explicit documentation that beava state contains no CDE-class data. PSD2 / PSD3 SCA + TRA — quarterly fraud-rate accounting under the EBA tiered thresholds (0.01% for €250–500, up to 0.13% for the lowest band; transactions >€500 always require SCA) must be exact and auditable. GDPR / CCPA — entity grains (merchant_id, card_hash, ip, device_id) include personal data; retention TTLs, right-to-erasure, and data-residency apply. SOC 2 Type II is table stakes for the orchestrator's enterprise customers, which pushes operational requirements onto beava (TLS, auth, audit log). NACHA / scheme rules (Visa VDMP / VFMP, Mastercard ECP) impose merchant fraud-rate thresholds that the orchestrator must monitor in real time.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: A single-acquirer success-rate dashboard with rolling 1m / 5m / 1h success-rate and latency p95 per (acquirer, BIN) can stand up in a few days on beava given the SDK's @bv.event / @bv.table primitives. A more realistic 50–80-feature production routing-feature substrate (per-acquirer health + per-(acquirer, BIN) approval-rate + per-merchant velocity + BIN-attack detection) integrated against a real charge stream is typically a 2–4 week effort. There is no `python/beava/demos/payments_orchestration/` directory in the repo today, so buyers would not have a runnable PSP-shaped vertical demo to start from.

competition.incumbents: Two layers. (a) Generic streaming / feature-store platforms used to build orchestrator routing rigs in-house: Redis (and managed Redis on AWS / Azure / GCP) is the dominant in-memory primitive — Lua scripts running atomic counters and token-bucket rate limiters on Redis is the canonical PSP velocity-counter pattern; Aerospike is the next tier up for very large card networks; Tecton (offers sub-millisecond feature lookups at >100k QPS, fraud reference); Chalk (explicitly lists 'Real-Time Payment Risk Decisioning' as a named use case — 'hundreds of fraud features per transaction in single-digit ms p99'); Feast (often on Redis); Hopsworks; Fennel; plus stream engines Flink, Materialize, RisingWave, Spark Structured Streaming, Confluent Flink. (b) Inside-orchestrator feature platforms built in-house: Stripe Shepherd (Chronon-based, ~200 features in SEPA Shepherd model). Beava competes most directly with the (Redis + Lua) + (Flink or Materialize) two-box pattern, by collapsing it into a single binary with 50+ first-class aggregation primitives.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Domain-specific orchestrators and routing-as-a-service vendors a buyer would otherwise procure as a black box rather than build on beava: Adyen RevenueAccelerate, Stripe Authorization Boost / Adaptive Acceptance, Checkout.com Intelligent Acceptance, Worldpay FraudSight (powered by Ravelin), JUSPAY Hyperswitch (open-source Rust), Primer, Gr4vy, Spreedly, Corefy, Solidgate, IXOPAY, Yuno, Cellulant, Nuvei, Paddle. Beava is not directly competing with these — it is the infrastructure substrate a buyer would use to build their own orchestrator or to augment an in-house routing stack. The closest 'feature-store-shaped' competitor in this domain is Chalk, which has explicitly productised 'Real-Time Payment Risk Decisioning' as a named use case.
competition.beava_differentiator: Five differentiators specific to this domain: (1) Single binary — no Kafka + Flink + Redis + feature-store ETL chain to operate inside the latency-sensitive routing path; PSP platform teams are not data-platform teams. (2) 50+ aggregation primitives covering counters, velocities, distances, rates, distributions — exactly the shape of per-(acquirer, BIN) rolling success-rate, per-acquirer latency distribution, per-(BIN, merchant) BIN-attack detection that PSP teams build by hand on top of Redis Lua scripts today. (3) Sub-ms TCP get / batch_get fits inside the 20–50 ms routing sub-budget with two orders of magnitude of headroom — Hyperswitch's whole application sits at ~25 ms total; beava's contribution would be <1 ms. (4) Push-on-event ingestion (HTTP/JSON, framed TCP, msgpack) maps cleanly to an orchestrator's existing webhook / gRPC connector responses without forcing a Kafka detour. (5) Apache-2.0 with no open-core — a PSP procurement team doesn't have to negotiate against a paid 'Enterprise Edition' two years in; the only direct open-source competitor in the orchestrator slot (Hyperswitch) is itself a routing engine, not a feature substrate, so beava is complementary to Hyperswitch rather than a competitor.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: Concrete gaps that will block production PSP/orchestrator deployments: (1) No TLS and no auth on :8080/:8081/:8090 — for a PSP this is a non-starter; auditors will block it even on a private subnet because of PCI-DSS network-segmentation requirements. (2) No in-process sharding — a global PSP's per-acquirer / per-(acquirer, BIN) state cannot be split across machines; vertical scaling only. (3) No cross-region replication — multi-region active-active orchestrators with EU + US + APAC authorization paths cannot use beava as the source of truth for gateway-health state without an external coordination layer. (4) In-memory only with refuse-on-network-FS — buyers must accept that all state is on local NVMe and a node loss requires WAL replay; regulator-grade PSD2 TRA accounting needs a downstream sink. (5) No triggers / no 'fire when counter crosses threshold' — the entire circuit-breaker / gateway-health pattern is 'when (acquirer, decline_code) decline-rate exceeds X in 60 s, open the breaker and re-route' — today this requires the buyer to poll beava, which loses the sub-200-ms switchover target the industry has set. (6) No multi-tenancy / no namespace ACLs — an orchestrator vendor (Primer, Gr4vy, Spreedly) cannot safely host multiple merchant tenants on one beava box, which is exactly their product shape. (7) No secondary indexes — 'find all merchants whose chargeback-rate exceeded 0.1% in the last 24 h' is a scan, not a primary-key get. (8) No native PII/token-field marking — PCI auditors will want explicit documentation that no PAN can land in beava state.
competition.integration_surface: Upstream producers in this domain are heterogeneous: the orchestrator's connector-response stream (typically internal gRPC or message queue — Kafka, RabbitMQ), the merchant's checkout webhook (HTTP push) at smaller buyers, scheme-network webhooks (Visa / Mastercard notifications), and the orchestrator's own gateway-health probe results. Beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 plus framed-TCP :8081 (JSON or msgpack) maps cleanly to the webhook and internal-gRPC paths once a thin shim is written; a native Kafka/Kinesis consumer is not in v0. Downstream consumers are: the routing engine itself (pulls features via batch_get inside the route-selection critical section), the ML scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM / increasingly transformer-based at large PSPs like Stripe), the gateway-health circuit-breaker, and operational dashboards.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. The buyer typically runs (a) a rules engine for hard merchant-level fraud-rate thresholds, scheme-rule velocity caps, and PSD2-TRA-eligibility gates, and (b) an ML routing model (often a multi-armed bandit / contextual bandit, sometimes XGBoost or a small neural ranker — Razorpay's published Smart Routing uses a contextual bandit; JUSPAY's published work is control-theoretic + RL + MAB) that consumes beava features. Beava is the feature substrate under both.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No publicly named beava users running this use case yet. Comparable published case studies that legitimise the shape of the problem: Stripe Adaptive Acceptance / Authorization Boost (recovers 10% of false declines, 'billions of dollars globally'; 1–2% auth uplift; 8% fraud reduction); Adyen RevenueAccelerate / Intelligent Payment Routing (26% cost savings, 0.22% auth uplift in 20-merchant enterprise pilot including eBay, 24 Hour Fitness, Microsoft); JUSPAY Hyperswitch (200M daily txns, $670B TPV, 99.999% reliability, control-theoretic routing paper 2025 showing ~1.15% improvement); Razorpay (2021 arXiv 'AI-powered Smart Routing'); Chalk's named 'Real-Time Payment Risk Decisioning' use case page documenting 'hundreds of fraud features per transaction in single-digit ms p99'; Stripe Shepherd (Chronon-based, ~200 features in SEPA fraud model, 'tens of millions of dollars of additional fraud blocked per year', 75% faster ML feature dev). Vendor reference customers for Adyen / Stripe / Checkout.com / Worldpay / Primer / Gr4vy / Spreedly are extensive but mostly private.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: [uncertain] No specific beava Discord / GitHub Discussion threads on PSP / orchestration routing identified in this research pass; the repo does not ship a payments-orchestration demo today.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No. There is no `python/beava/demos/payments_orchestration/` directory in the repo today. The existing `python/beava/demos/fraud/` directory covers the issuer-/merchant-side CNP fraud shape (item 1a), not the orchestrator-side routing shape; the events.jsonl there contains charge / decline events but not route_request / route_decision / gateway_response / retry_attempt events. A dedicated payments-orchestration demo would be a productive add: schema for {route_request, route_decision, gateway_response, retry_attempt} plus tables for per-(acquirer, BIN) approval-rate, per-acquirer latency p95, and (BIN, merchant) BIN-attack counters.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: High / active adversary plus high passive load. The BIN-attack and card-testing surface is as adversarial as item 1a (fraudsters adapt within hours, rotate IPs and devices, deliberately stay under per-identifier thresholds). The routing / gateway-health surface is more passive-load — acquirer outages and decline-pattern shifts are not adversarial actors, but they are stochastic and high-velocity, which puts the same freshness pressure on the feature substrate.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: Beava is the wrong tool for: (1) Storing PAN, CVV, or any sensitive authentication data — that belongs in the orchestrator's token vault; beava only sees tokens. (2) Long historical lookbacks (60–180 day per-merchant routing-policy training data — that belongs in a warehouse / lakehouse / offline feature store, Tecton's offline tier, Snowflake, or Databricks). (3) Full event archive for regulatory replay (PSD2 fraud-rate accounting evidentiary trails, chargeback-evidence packages — these need years; beava's role is hot-path aggregation, not system of record). (4) Cross-entity joins ('all merchants whose chargeback-rate > 0.1% AND volume > $X AND MCC = Y') — beava is keyed by primary entity, not a query engine; that belongs in the analytics tier. (5) Batch routing-model training and offline backfill — Spark / Snowflake / Databricks. (6) Multi-tenant hosting by an orchestrator vendor without namespace ACLs (no multi-tenancy in v0). (7) Heavy multi-region active-active deployments without an external coordination layer (no cross-region replication in v0).
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava needs to ship to be production-grade for PSP/orchestrator routing/risk at a mid-to-large buyer: (1) TLS on all three listeners (:8080, :8081, :8090) plus mTLS option — PCI-DSS network segmentation will not certify cleartext on an internal subnet. (2) AuthN/AuthZ — API-key auth scoped per namespace at minimum, ideally JWT / OIDC and per-namespace RBAC. (3) Triggers / event-driven actions — 'when (acquirer, decline_code) counter crosses threshold T in window W, emit an action event to a webhook or Kafka topic' — gateway-health circuit-breaking is the textbook trigger use case; today the buyer must poll and loses the <200 ms switchover target the industry has set. (4) Multi-tenancy with hard namespace isolation, per-tenant quotas, and per-tenant auth — orchestrator vendors host many merchant tenants on one platform. (5) In-process sharding / consistent-hashing for entities so vertical limits do not cap a global PSP. (6) Cross-region replication (active-active or active-passive with bounded staleness) for global authorization paths. (7) Approximate-aggregate primitives surfaced first-class: HLL n_unique, CMS top-K, t-digest for latency distribution per acquirer. (8) Secondary indexes / scan APIs — 'top-N merchants by chargeback-rate in last 24 h', 'top-N (BIN, merchant) by attempt-velocity in last 5 min' — needed for ops dashboards and hunter queries. (9) Configurable per-feature TTLs and eviction so 90-day TRA-accounting accumulators coexist with 1-minute health windows. (10) Explicit PII / token-field marking, an audit log, and a published 'beava is out of CDE scope' posture document so the buyer can pass PCI-DSS v4.0.1 and SOC 2 audits without manual evidence collection. (11) A durable downstream sink (Kafka / Postgres CDC / S3 out) so PSD2 TRA fraud-rate accounting is independently auditable against a system of record. (12) Cost-aware aggregation primitives (rolling cost-per-successful-auth per route) and explicit support for percentile aggregates per acquirer (p50/p95/p99 latency over rolling window).
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes, this is the single strongest pull for the trigger/action gap in beava's roadmap. The circuit-breaker pattern that drives the entire PSP gateway-health story is fundamentally 'when (acquirer, decline_code) decline-rate exceeds X in 60 s, emit an action event so the routing layer opens the breaker.' Industry best-in-class targets sub-200 ms switchover from detection to re-route. Beava's current poll-only model cannot hit that target without the trigger primitive — this is a blocking gap for productionising this use case.
